analysis.one_liner: Caps big trucks at 65 mph by requiring speed-limiting devices on new commercial trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Transportation Department to set rules within a year making speed-limiting devices mandatory equipment on all new heavy trucks (over 26,000 pounds) and requiring any speed limiter already built into trucks made after 1992 to actually be used, with a top speed of 65 mph (or 70 mph if the truck has automatic emergency braking and adaptive cruise control). The bill's stated basis was federal data showing more than 10,000 deaths over a decade in crashes where a commercial truck's speed likely made the outcome worse.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who shares the road with large trucks — drivers of passenger cars, cyclists, and pedestrians — plus truck drivers themselves, since a majority of surveyed drivers told the Insurance Institute they favored speed limiters. Slower trucks mean fewer and less severe crashes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone sharing the road with heavy trucks

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs NHTSA to require speed-limiting technology on all new commercial vehicles over 26,001 pounds, capped at 65 mph, or 70 mph only when paired with automatic emergency braking and adaptive cruise control [S2][S3].
It also requires trucks built after 1992 that already have speed limiters installed to actually use them, closing a gap where devices exist but drivers can override them [S2][S3].

The bill's findings cite federal data of 10,440 deaths from 2004 to 2013 in crashes where truck speed likely contributed to severity, and a 2012 federal-commissioned study finding trucks without speed limiters had nearly double the speed-relevant crash rate [S3].
The bill's findings note 64 percent of surveyed truck drivers supported a speed-limiting requirement, and that the UK, EU, and Australia have mandated such devices for 25-30 years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies would bear compliance costs and slightly slower delivery times, though speed limiters also cut fuel use. Fleet owners and owner-operators who profit by covering highway miles as fast as possible would lose the most. Truck buyers would ultimately absorb the cost of the required equipment in vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Truckers paid by the mile, especially owner-operators, could see their effective earnings reduced if they are legally unable to keep up with faster traffic flow on high-speed-limit highways — a cost the bill does not address [S3].

Requiring only 65 mph regardless of posted speed limits could create speed differentials between trucks and cars on rural interstates with 70-75 mph limits, which safety researchers debate as a possible source of more car-truck interactions [S3].
Compliance certification falls on vehicle owners, adding paperwork and enforcement questions the bill leaves to later regulation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety benefit is backed by the bill's own findings — federal crash data and international precedent — and it fits technology that most large trucks already have installed. The main real costs fall on trucking businesses in slower trips and on drivers paid by the mile, not on the general public. On balance the design is straightforward and the tradeoff favors the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees in May 2021 and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath (D-GA) introduced the bill on May 25, 2021, joined by Rep. John Katko (R-NY), making it a bipartisan introduction [S1][S3].

The same day, it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee; the next day it went to the Highways and Transit and Consumer Protection and Commerce subcommittees [S5].
No further action was ever taken — the bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].
Only one Republican cosponsor signed on over the bill's lifetime [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies and owner-operators that oppose speed limiters avoided any mandate to cap speeds at 65 mph, and no manufacturer faced a new equipment requirement. Road users gained nothing; the crash risk the bill cited remained unaddressed by this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking operators who opposed speed caps

for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill's provisions within its jurisdiction, which covered the vehicle-equipment standard.

against.name: Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association
against.role: Association of small trucking firms and owner-operators
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal speed-limiter mandates, arguing they hurt small operators paid by the mile; large segments of the trucking industry have historically lobbied against similar NHTSA rules.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican cosponsor, but only 1 Republican cosponsor ever signed on, and the Democratic-led committees that held it never scheduled any action.

industries.note: A 65 mph cap means slower trips and less revenue per truck per day for carriers that plan around faster highway speeds. The public benefit — fewer and less severe crashes — comes directly at their operating model's expense, though carriers also save on fuel at lower speeds.
Drivers paid by the mile lose the most per hour from a speed cap, and this segment of the industry has historically opposed federal speed-limiter mandates.

A mandate that every new heavy truck carry speed limiters, automatic emergency braking, and adaptive cruise control creates a guaranteed market for that equipment. The public safety benefit and the manufacturers' revenue both come from the same requirement.
